extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary criticism; poets, critics, and educated general readers interested in evaluating Romantic poetry and public speaking
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging the qualities of Wordsworthian/Romantic poetry (and related remarks on lecturing/oratory), including style, subject-matter, imaginative power, finish, and audience-appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of truth and feeling (natural over artificial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should be founded on 'an absolute essence of truth and feeling' and anything professing to be more is 'vitiated, false, and spurious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt frames Wordsworth's principle as setting up an opposition 'between the natural and the artificial; between the spirit of humanity, and the spirit of fashion and of the world.' Poetry ought to avoid affectedness and artifice and aim for genuine feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levelling Muse / Equality of subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The Muse 'proceeds on a principle of equality, and strives to reduce all things to the same standard' by taking common events/objects as proper poetic subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the commonest events and objects to show that 'nature is always interesting from its inherent truth and beauty, without any of the ornaments of dress or pomp of circumstances to set it off.' This is tied to rejecting pomp and artificial subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and inartificial style
rubrics_metrics.description: A popular, inartificial style that discards the 'trappings of verse' and traditional pomp (e.g., 'cloud-capt towers', odes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ornate classical forms (Ode, Epode, Strophe) and theatrical ornamentation; prefer plain diction and economy of decorative devices. Hazlitt cites the Lyrical Ballads as exemplifying this simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of trivial incidents as vehicles for reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects or stories should serve 'merely as pegs or loops to hang thought and feeling on'; incidents may be trifling in service of deeper reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the reflective, philosophical content over spectacular incident; incidents are functional rather than ends in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevation of the mean by imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'elevates the mean by the strength of his own aspirations; he clothes the naked with beauty and grandeur from the stores of his own recollections.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imaginative power should transform humble, ordinary objects into sources of grandeur and feeling; the poet's inner resources supply the grandeur rather than external pomp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of spectacular horror in favor of subtle emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should favor subtle natural emotional moments ('the dew-drop glitters', 'the tear collects') rather than sensational catastrophes (storms, shipwrecks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on delicate, interior feeling and small natural phenomena as loci of poetic meaning instead of dramatic sensational events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of association with place and memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry often springs from habit and familiarity with pastoral scenes; each object becomes 'connected with a thousand feelings' and a 'link in the chain of thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal/communal associations (memory, place) to imbue mundane objects with emotional density; intimate knowledge of landscape enriches poetic feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality — offering new views of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving 'a new view or aspect of nature' and an intensity of feeling previously undisplayed marks originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek a distinctive voice that presents familiar things in fresh ways; Hazlitt calls Wordsworth 'the most original poet now living' for this capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity combined with profundity (seeming simplicity and real abstruseness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works may appear simple yet contain deep, abstruse reflections—'Fools have laughed at, wise men scarcely understand them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for surface simplicity that conceals intellectual depth; accept that some readers will miss subtler meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholeness / unity of design (especially in landscape and art)
rubrics_metrics.description: A landscape or composition 'must express the time of day, the climate, the period of the world it was meant to illustrate' — a 'wholeness in it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works for an internal unity of design: all parts should cohere to create a convincing, contextual whole (Hazlitt uses Poussin as example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative transmutation (making ideal from common)
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist/poet should 'work something out of nothing, and transform the stump of a tree, a common figure into an ideal object' (Rembrandt analogy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the creator's ability to endow ordinary details with an 'atmosphere of sentiment' that renders them idealized and expressive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish and polish appropriate to the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Later philosophic poems are 'polished in style...the perfection of the finishing, like that of careful sculpture' — a smooth, solid 'texture of the thoughts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value careful finishing where suitable: clarity, solidity, and polished phrasing can be virtues (Hazlitt praises Laodamia for this quality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate balance of vigor and restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophic poetry may have 'less tumult' but an impression that is 'more pleading and permanent' — restraint can produce lasting effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure whether intensity is modulated appropriately: vivid tumult versus calm, pleading permanence — different effects suit different aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and coherence of structure (avoid repetition and overlength)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works like The Excursion fail by being 'long and laboured', repeating conclusions till they become 'flat and insipid' and raising expectations not fulfilled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for concision, coherent plan, variation of treatment, and fulfillment of promises; avoid unnecessary length and repetitive reiteration of the same principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit between subject and scale/treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan of a work must match its subject and audience; ill-judged scale makes effects ludicrous (e.g., a 'splendid banquet in the company of clowns' with apple-dumplings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure tone, register, and scale are congruent; don't present humble material with inappropriate grandiosity or vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral delivery and performative effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's manner of reading and presence can be necessary to convey the full idea of the poetry — 'the comment of his face and voice is necessary to convey a full idea of his poetry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating performance or reception, consider how recitation, voice, and personal presence shape the audience's understanding of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between passion and reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet condemns 'dry reasoners' for want of passion and is 'jealous of the rhetorical declaimers' for trenching on poetry's province.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value passionate feeling in poetry but beware rhetorical excess that moves into declamation; seek an authentic blend where feeling powers thought without mere rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generosity and breadth of critical sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive fastidiousness leads to narrowness, intolerance, and worse reception; 'if Mr. Wordsworth had been a more liberal and candid critic, he would have been a more sterling writer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical openness and willingness to draw from many sources broaden a writer's appeal and strengthen work; avoid doctrinaire exclusiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lasting emotional impact vs. transient effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should either leave a 'mark behind them that never wears out' rather than making no impression or a transient one that 'falls blunted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether a work's effects are merely momentary or enduring; aim for sentiments that persist rather than immediate fireworks alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of standards and moderation in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Too severe or exclusive standards ('admits of nothing below, scarcely of any thing above himself') narrow judgment and alienate readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain fair, moderate standards and avoid dismissing whole traditions wholesale; learned severity should not become dogmatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate adaptation to audience and medium (oratory)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a political partisan Sir James is 'the lecturer rather than the advocate' — fine in a neutral, impartial assembly but liable to fail in a partisan House of Commons where passion and tactical concision matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor argument and style to venue: academic/lecturing style (comprehensive, logical, many exceptions) may be unsuited to parliamentary/partisan contexts that demand unity, force, and tactical brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of purpose and energetic delivery (public speaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oratory must have 'unity of purpose, impetuosity of feeling to break through the phalanx of hostile and inveterate prejudice' — excessive concessions neutralize an argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-qualification, needless concessions, and exhaustive listing of pros/cons that let opponents pick holes; favour clear decisive thrusts in contentious public speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding excessive appeal to authorities (writing style)
rubrics_metrics.description: In writing Sir James 'overlays the original subject and spirit of the composition, by an appeal to authorities and by too formal a method.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not smother original thought under a weight of citations and overly formal structure; preserve the central subject and spirit of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain prudence alongside confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Dazzling success in lecture can lead to loss of prudence — 'He grew wanton with success...lost fear as well as prudence; dared every thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance confidence with caution; rhetorical daring should not compromise judgment or invite unnecessary error.
